title: Save Jjs

jokes.text: They're all so good, I can't pick just two. / Well, then you leave, Terry. And pay for the cake you already ate.
jokes.setup: Terry expresses genuine enthusiasm about all the cakes, unable to narrow it down
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately dismisses him and demands payment, treating his sentiment as a liability
jokes.explanation: Classic Terry/Leslie dynamic: Terry's earnest enthusiasm is weaponized against him. The line 'pay for the cake you already ate' is economical and mean in the perfect Parks way. Strong character integration — this works because it's Leslie running a tight ship AND because Terry is always the butt of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Terry, we don't have time for this. You're getting the first cake. I'm going to go get my checkbook.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You owe me $47.

jokes.text: I like the vanilla one with the lemon cream. / That was a joke cake I got from the grocery store, to weed out low-quality palates.
jokes.setup: Someone identifies a grocery store cake as their favorite
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals it was a deliberate test cake to expose bad taste — a trap for low-quality palates
jokes.explanation: A well-structured misdirection: the grocery store cake being good is relatable, but it's a trap. 'To weed out low-quality palates' is a wonderfully pretentious phrase. The rewatch bonus is real — knowing Leslie put a grocery store cake in a blind taste test to judge people adds a layer of delightful characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you actually liked that vanilla cake with lemon cream? That was a test cake to eliminate people with bad taste.

jokes.text: Maybe it's because he's my fiancé and I love him, but I kind of like the grocery store one, too.
jokes.setup: The grocery store cake has been exposed as a low-quality trap
jokes.punchline: Donna, the fiancée, admits she also likes the grocery store cake, undermining the entire premise while offering a loving excuse
jokes.explanation: Immediate callback that lands by having Donna also fail the test, but her framing ('maybe it's because he's my fiancé') softens it with warmth. The comedy is in how love excuses bad taste — a gentle, character-specific beat.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I like it too.

jokes.text: Donna has chosen me to be the Butler of Honor at her wedding. Now, granted, 'Butler of Honor' is a term I made up, but it's not a job I take lightly.
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining his role at Donna's wedding in a talking-head confessional
jokes.punchline: He invented the title 'Butler of Honor' himself, then immediately insists it's a serious responsibility
jokes.explanation: Highly character-specific: Tom inventing a title for himself and then earnestly defending it is pure Tom Haverford. 'Butler of Honor' is an absurd term that somehow sounds exactly right for him. The immediate pivot to 'it's not a job I take lightly' is the perfect deadpan self-awareness. Strong character integration score because no other character on the show could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm the best maid of honor.

jokes.text: DJ Bluntz surprise reveal — Tom presents Donna with a surprise bigger than when LeBron went back to Miami
jokes.setup: Tom builds up a mysterious surprise as bigger than a major cultural moment (LeBron's return to Miami)
jokes.punchline: The reveal is DJ Bluntz, which makes Donna completely lose it in joy while Tom basks in credit
jokes.explanation: The LeBron comparison as a hyperbolic benchmark is a nice touch, and Donna's genuine reaction pays off the build. The joke works mainly on character energy. The sports analogy dates the episode but fits Tom's voice well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a huge surprise for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: LeBron James is going back to Miami!

jokes.text: Treat Yo' Self. Treat Yo' Self 2017! / Oh, my God! Is this for real? Oh, it's for real. And it's the biggest one yet. / I still don't know what's happening. So, what's happening? Treat Yo' Self. Not an answer to my question.
jokes.setup: Tom and Donna announce 'Treat Yo' Self 2017' with full fanfare; Terry has been present the whole time
jokes.punchline: Terry's repeated genuine confusion ('Not an answer to my question') as everyone around him has a transcendent experience
jokes.explanation: The Treat Yo' Self callback is always crowd-pleasing for established fans. What elevates this iteration is Terry's persistent genuine confusion cutting through the celebration. 'Not an answer to my question' is the best line of the sequence — it's perfectly logical and completely ignored. Rewatch bonus for series fans recognizing the callback.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Every year, without fail, it happens.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self.

jokes.text: Terry, what's happening? Treat Yo' Self. It's the best day of the year! / Read the cake. Still unclear.
jokes.setup: Everyone keeps saying 'Treat Yo' Self' as an explanation; Terry is directed to the cake
jokes.punchline: Reading the cake ('Treat Yo' Self') still provides no clarity to Terry — 'Still unclear.'
jokes.explanation: 'Still unclear' is perfectly economical — two words that puncture the entire celebratory atmosphere. The joke escalates the running gag of using Treat Yo' Self as a non-answer by having even a physical object (the cake) fail to communicate the concept to Terry.

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: What's happening? What is going on?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self!

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: No, seriously, what's happening right now?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self!

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: Can someone please just tell me what is going on?!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self!

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: WHAT IS HAPPENING?!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self.

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: I hate all of you!

jokes.text: We did not believe that we did anything to invade people's privacy. But then, we checked thousands of emails and texts between our customers and their loved ones, and it seemed like people thought we were wrong.
jokes.setup: Roscoe (Gryzzl rep) is asked if they've done anything wrong regarding data mining
jokes.punchline: They discovered people thought they were wrong by... reading their private communications — the exact thing they're being accused of
jokes.explanation: This is the sharpest joke in the episode and earns its 8+ score. The structure is airtight: the defense of their privacy invasion is itself an admission of further privacy invasion. It's a perfect logical loop that satirizes tech company tone-deafness with precision. 'It seemed like people thought we were wrong' is a masterpiece of corporate doublespeak — they can't even acknowledge wrongdoing directly. Highly quotable and genuinely smart writing.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: We would never invade anyone's privacy.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: Well, I checked 47,000 private emails this morning, but that's just routine.

jokes.text: We are gonna be throwing a free concert with U2 and Beyoncé. Tickets are already on your phones, seating is gonna be organized by income and sexual history.
jokes.setup: Gryzzl announces a PR stunt concert to win back public trust
jokes.punchline: The concert seating is organized by income and sexual history — using exactly the kind of private data they promised to stop accessing
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured: the apology concert itself uses the data they claim to stop using. 'Sexual history' as a seating category is the absurdist escalation that takes it from clever to genuinely funny. The joke indicts tech company PR without ever winking at the audience — Roscoe says it with complete earnestness. Near-excellent writing.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Representative
dialogue.line: We'd like to make it up to you with a free concert! We've arranged special seating based on our extensive data about you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what kind of seating arrangement?

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Representative
dialogue.line: Well, we know you like to sit alone, so we've placed you in an isolated section. We know Leslie prefers to be near the front and center of attention, so she's up there. And Roscoe, we've seated you next to people who share your exact browsing history.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: How is that possible? That's incredibly invasive!

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Representative
dialogue.line: We know everything about you. Everything.

jokes.text: And that, I swear, is the last time that we will be peeking inside your computers.
jokes.setup: Roscoe is wrapping up the apology, promising to stop the data mining
jokes.punchline: Uses the childish word 'peeking' to describe corporate data surveillance, trivializing the violation
jokes.explanation: 'Peeking' does a lot of work here — it's deliberately infantile language for something invasive. Good character voice work: Roscoe speaks in a language that makes violations sound innocuous. Solid but slightly outshone by the bigger Gryzzl jokes around it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've got it! We use multiple blimps!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, why would we need multiple blimps?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know, but it sounds awesome!

jokes.text: I've got something big and exciting. All we need is a blimp and a decoy blimp.
jokes.setup: Leslie calls for big and exciting ideas in the land battle strategy meeting
jokes.punchline: Andy's plan involves a blimp AND a decoy blimp, as if the decoy blimp is the detail that makes it actionable
jokes.explanation: Pure Andy Dwyer energy. The genius is the 'decoy blimp' — it implies some complex operational thinking behind an utterly useless plan. The specificity of two blimps (one real, one decoy) makes it more absurd than just saying 'a blimp.' Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What about blimps?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, we've talked about this. Multiple times. Blimps are not a viable transportation solution for our parks department.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But they're so cool.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know you think they're cool. That's the problem. That's always the problem.

jokes.text: Okay. For what I hope is the last time, but we'll assume is not the last time, our strategy does not involve blimps.
jokes.setup: Andy has suggested blimps as a strategy
jokes.punchline: Leslie's exhausted parenthetical — 'we'll assume is not the last time' — reveals this is a recurring problem
jokes.explanation: The self-aware parenthetical is the joke — Leslie knows this won't be the last time she has to say this. It's efficient storytelling and comedy simultaneously. The acknowledgment that she'll have to repeat herself suggests a long history of Andy's blimp ideas.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Walker
dialogue.line: I need to give you my standard disclaimer. Everything you tell me is classified information. You cannot share it with anyone, not your family, not your friends, not even your therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Even my therapist? That seems like a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Walker
dialogue.line: Especially your therapist. They're a person.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, I'm aware of what a therapist is.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Walker
dialogue.line: Then you understand the risk.

jokes.text: I am not a spy, and I would never reveal classified information. / Do you have to say that every time? / Yes.
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie are discussing their plan; Ron apparently always denies being a spy
jokes.punchline: Leslie asks if he has to say it every time; Ron says yes — no explanation given, no deviation
jokes.explanation: Beautiful Ron Swanson economy. The exchange is three lines and tells you everything about Ron's character: the ritual denial, Leslie's weary familiarity, and Ron's unblinking 'Yes' — which raises more questions than it answers. Why does he have to say it every time? We'll never know, and that's funnier. Near-perfect economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron and I are like Justin Timberlake and Chris Kirkpatrick from NSYNC.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You mean the band NSYNC?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, I said Justin Timberlake and Chris Kirkpatrick.

jokes.text: And just like Joey Fatone and Lance Bass, we are totally in sync. Come on. / We're in sync emotionally. Stop patting my head.
jokes.setup: Leslie is celebrating her reunited partnership with Ron, making a *NSYNC reference
jokes.punchline: The *NSYNC pun ('in sync' / *NSYNC) lands with Leslie physically patting Ron's head, which he immediately shuts down
jokes.explanation: The *NSYNC pun is low-key clever — Leslie picking the two least-famous members of the band (Fatone and Bass rather than Timberlake) is a nice detail that speaks to her character. Ron's disgust at the head-patting is the physical comedy payoff. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Ron, we're going to do a synchronized dance to show how in-sync we are as a department.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, it'll be fun! Just follow my lead.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would rather sit through a city council meeting where they discuss parking regulations for three hours.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's your favorite thing!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Let me repeat that because it makes me very horny. C'mon, Knope. $125 million.
jokes.setup: The Newport Trust rep announces they're selling to Gryzzl for $125 million despite their stated principles
jokes.punchline: He repeats the number because saying it aloud arouses him — a jarring, absurd admission of greed
jokes.explanation: 'It makes me very horny' is a genuinely surprising non-sequitur from a suit-and-tie character. The shock of a corporate rep being this openly id-driven lands as absurdist. 'C'mon, Knope' as a dismissal of her moral objection while he savors his own arousal is pitch-perfect. Quotable and punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Newport Trust Representative
dialogue.line: The sale price is $47 million.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I need to go take a cold shower.

jokes.text: In case something happens to you, I wanna make sure I get paid. / Looking out for number one. Always smart.
jokes.setup: Tom is about to leave; an employee asks him to sign checks and requests to go first
jokes.punchline: The reason for going first is survival-based pragmatism — in case Tom dies before signing — and Tom endorses this logic without missing a beat
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient gag. The employee's ruthless self-interest is funny; Tom's approval makes it a workplace commentary. Not a standout but does its job cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I need you to sign these checks so that if you die, I'll still get paid.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's... actually a very practical concern.

jokes.text: Well, breakups are famously super fun and make everyone feel awesome. So, it's no different.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Tom how post-breakup life is going
jokes.punchline: Tom deploys thick sarcasm ('famously super fun') while maintaining the deadpan delivery of a man in denial
jokes.explanation: Functional sarcasm. 'Famously super fun' is a decent phrase. Not particularly novel — the deflecting sarcasm about a breakup is a well-worn sitcom move — but Tom's specific energy makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, it's great. I'm sleeping on a futon in the back of my office at Entertainment 720, I'm eating nothing but protein bars and sadness, and I've started a journal where I write angry letters to my ex that I'll never send. So yeah, living the dream.

jokes.text: You should come to the wedding and do paperwork. Stop, you're making this sound almost too fun.
jokes.setup: Donna suggests Tom bring Lucy to the wedding; Tom is awkward; Donna suggests he come as boss-employee doing paperwork
jokes.punchline: Tom's deadpan response ('almost too fun') — the sarcasm cuts through his romantic paralysis with comic timing
jokes.explanation: Solid banter. 'Almost too fun' is efficient and dry. Works as romantic subplot comedy but doesn't transcend the genre.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April, I wanted to ask you something. Would you maybe want to come to my wedding? As a guest? With a plus-one if you want?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom, that's sweet, but I'm probably going to be pretty busy that day.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, okay, I understand. Well, actually, we could really use some help with parking and setup, so maybe you could come as staff?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, I can do that.

jokes.text: Whatever, just text me when you decide. I literally couldn't care less. So, yeah. Let's hit it, Donna.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to be cool about whether Lucy comes to the wedding
jokes.punchline: His rapid exit — 'I literally couldn't care less. So, yeah. Let's hit it, Donna' — is transparently the opposite of not caring
jokes.explanation: Tom's very obvious lie that he doesn't care, punctuated by an immediate pivot to Donna, is a reliable comic beat. Works because it's real — Tom's bravado is always a thin veneer.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wow, Tom. You've made paperwork sound so fun. I can't believe I haven't been doing it at every social event for years.

jokes.text: Today is about one thing. Things, Donna! Our favorite.
jokes.setup: Tom insists today is about Treat Yo' Self and nothing else
jokes.punchline: He says today is about 'one thing' then immediately corrects himself — 'Things' — because Treat Yo' Self is by definition about many things
jokes.explanation: A small but well-constructed self-correction gag. Tom's excitement undermines his own philosophy. 'Things, Donna! Our favorite.' is delivered with infectious energy. Clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just text me about the wedding decision, okay?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't care about weddings. They're boring and pointless.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So you won't text me?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I'll text you. But only because I have nothing better to do.

jokes.text: Treat Yo' Self in Beverly Hills! (reveal)
jokes.setup: Tom has been building to something beyond the mall for Treat Yo' Self
jokes.punchline: The reveal is Beverly Hills — the most extravagant possible escalation of the Treat Yo' Self concept
jokes.explanation: A solid reveal moment that works primarily as fan service and escalation of the running gag. Beverly Hills is a logical but delightfully over-the-top destination for Tom and Donna. The rewatch bonus applies for fans of the arc.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Treat Yo' Self is about doing whatever makes you happy. For some people it's eating cupcakes, for other people it's going to the spa, but the common thread is things. We both love things.

jokes.text: All I wanted was 25 square miles of land valued at $100 million given to me for free. Is that too much to ask?
jokes.setup: Leslie is lamenting the loss of the land deal
jokes.punchline: She describes her ask as if it were modest and reasonable — 100-million-dollar land gifted for free
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's complete lack of self-awareness about the scale of her ask, framed as a plaintive 'is that too much?' The specific numbers make the absurdity precise. Good Leslie characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so we've been perfecting this tradition for years, right?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The best tradition.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And we've decided to take it to the next level. We're doing Treat Yo'self... at the mall.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The ultimate consumer destination.

jokes.text: I'll say it again. Voodoo is still an option.
jokes.setup: Leslie is declaring defeat; someone is trying to comfort or advise her
jokes.punchline: 'I'll say it again' implies this has been offered before and rejected; offering voodoo as a serious strategic option
jokes.explanation: 'I'll say it again' does the heavy lifting — it implies an ongoing commitment to voodoo as a plan that has been repeatedly dismissed. Brief but has charm. Character attribution is unclear from transcript context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just want something small and simple. Nothing fancy. Just a little 500-person gala with live music, a seven-course meal, and appearances by every celebrity who has ever lived.

jokes.text: And there's too much kale now. One place asked me if I wanted kale in my milkshake. My milkshake, you guys.
jokes.setup: Character is reflecting on changes in Pawnee — some positive, some not
jokes.punchline: The kale-in-milkshake detail lands as the final, unforgivable indignity; 'My milkshake, you guys' is an appeal to shared outrage
jokes.explanation: 'My milkshake, you guys' is the line that makes this joke — the shift to a conspiratorial, almost wounded appeal to the camera. It's observational comedy that taps into genuine foodie-culture fatigue. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe we lost the land. This is the worst thing that's ever happened.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You could always put a curse on them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I can't curse people.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Even though I'm a firm believer in the free market, and your failure as a businessman is ultimately to blame, it's still a travesty your diner is closing.
jokes.setup: Ron is expressing sympathy to JJ about the diner closing
jokes.punchline: Ron's condolences are inseparable from his libertarian ideology — he literally cannot offer comfort without assigning blame and invoking the free market
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Ron Swanson writing. The joke only works because of deep character specificity — Ron cannot express sympathy without filtering it through his libertarian worldview. 'Your failure as a businessman is ultimately to blame' delivered in the same tone as 'it's still a travesty' is pitch-perfect. It's both a character joke AND a critique of ideology, packed into two sentences. Earns its 8.0 craft score: comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example, with strong economy, earned character integration, and surprising structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There's too much kale in Pawnee. It's everywhere. And now someone's put kale in my milkshake. A milkshake! That's a violation of milkshake sanctity!

jokes.text: Was it Putin? Voldemort Putin, of Russia? I'd love to take that bastard down.
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking who the new landlord is that bought JJ's property
jokes.punchline: Andy's guess is 'Voldemort Putin, of Russia' — combining two cultural villains into one invented person, plus 'of Russia' as if there's another Putin they might mean
jokes.explanation: 'Voldemort Putin, of Russia' is a genuinely funny name-mashup. The 'of Russia' clarification is the best part — as if Andy is distinguishing him from another Putin they know. His immediate eagerness to take him down rounds out the pure Andy Dwyer character beat. Well-constructed absurdist gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: JJ, I know this is hard. But you have to understand, this is your fault.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You didn't work hard enough. You didn't manage your money well enough. And frankly, your food was mediocre at best.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But the good news is, now you can start over. And this time, you'll fail faster.

jokes.text: Thigh Gap, LLC. Owner, Dennis Feinstein. / The cologne guy? Ugh, figures. That guy is the worst.
jokes.setup: The mystery landlord is about to be revealed
jokes.punchline: 'Thigh Gap, LLC' as a company name is absurd on its face; the reveal of Dennis Feinstein (established villain) adds satisfaction
jokes.explanation: 'Thigh Gap, LLC' is a great throwaway gag — it tells you everything about Dennis Feinstein with no explanation needed. The reveal of a known antagonist is satisfying for returning viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So who's your landlord?

dialogue.speaker: JJ
dialogue.line: His name is Earl Snoodle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Earl Snoodle? That sounds like a villain from a made-up movie.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. Tiny rolled-up scrolls delivered by trained foxes. I'm on it.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks April to spread the word using whatever communication methods young people use
jokes.punchline: April responds with a completely absurd, pre-industrial method (fox-delivered scrolls) stated in a completely flat, professional tone
jokes.explanation: This is the funniest April Ludgate joke in the episode. The setup (Leslie's generational condescension about 'what young people use') invites a response about social media — instead April weaponizes absurdism with perfect deadpan delivery. 'I'm on it' is the killer closer, treating fox-delivered scrolls as totally actionable. Economy score is near-perfect: maximum comedy per word. Earns its 8.0 — comparable to the anchor example in precision and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, what's the best way to reach young people? You know, use whatever communication method young people use these days.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Snapchat.

jokes.text: Andy, you thinking what I'm thinking? / Oh, hell, yeah. Blimp time. / No.
jokes.setup: Leslie is setting up a call-to-action; Andy completes her thought
jokes.punchline: Andy's answer is 'Blimp time' — after Leslie already shot down his blimp idea. Her 'No.' is instantaneous.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback delivery. The structure is airtight: the 'you thinking what I'm thinking?' setup creates a false intimacy, Andy immediately proves he's on a completely different page, and Leslie's 'No.' lands like a hammer. Three words total for the exchange and it works beautifully. Blimp joke gets a second life by being the WRONG answer to an invitation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Still convinced everything involves blimps

jokes.text: I think this is a job for Jonathan Karate. / Awesome. Even better.
jokes.setup: After rejecting blimps, Leslie pivots to 'Jonathan Karate' as the solution
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'Awesome. Even better.' — he has no idea what Jonathan Karate is but is immediately on board
jokes.explanation: Andy's wholehearted endorsement of something he clearly doesn't understand is pure character comedy. 'Even better' than blimps is a great detail — he's still ranking it against blimps in his head.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. A blimp? That's not gonna work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I need to switch to my serious character. Bud Stubbins.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Bud Stubbins doesn't do blimps. Bud Stubbins does real police work.

jokes.text: I can't think of anything more noble to go to war over than bacon and eggs.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron if he's in for one more fight to save JJ's Diner
jokes.punchline: Ron's most sincere statement of the episode — unironically declaring breakfast food worthy of war
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson and among the best lines in the episode. The joke is that he's entirely serious — there's no irony in Ron's voice when he says this. His hierarchy of values (bacon > most things) is perfectly consistent with everything we know about him. 'Nothing more noble to go to war over than bacon and eggs' is highly quotable and earns its craft score. Economical, perfectly characterized, and genuinely warm under the absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Breakfast food is the foundation of civilization. Waffles, eggs, bacon — these aren't just meals, they're statements of purpose. A man who fights to save a diner is a man fighting for the soul of this community. I'm in.

jokes.text: Well, we'll keep practicing. (implied trombone practice fail before rally)
jokes.setup: A brief scene apparently showing someone failing at trombone practice
jokes.punchline: 'Well, we'll keep practicing' — the understatement implies the performance was bad
jokes.explanation: Context is limited from the transcript alone. Works as a brief transitional gag but with no setup visible in the transcript, it's hard to score highly. Functional but weak without visual context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We nailed it!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We did not nail it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But we were so close! I could feel the synergy.

jokes.text: And this man, right here, built that diner from the ground up, with his own two hands. / That's not true. / It's called 'constructing a narrative,' JJ. You stick to the breakfast, I'll deal with the politics.
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving a rally speech mythologizing JJ's history with the diner
jokes.punchline: JJ immediately and flatly contradicts her; Leslie's response is to label it 'constructing a narrative' and assign JJ to his lane
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharper jokes. Leslie's instant pivot from caught-in-a-lie to 'constructing a narrative' is a pitch-perfect satire of political spin. 'You stick to the breakfast, I'll deal with the politics' is the killer line — she's shameless and efficient. The division of labor she's proposing is exactly how politicians actually work. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I didn't build it myself. But I'm going to tell people I did.

dialogue.speaker: JJ
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because the truth is boring. 'A bunch of people worked together on a project.' Where's the narrative? Where's the hero's journey? I'm creating a better story.

jokes.text: I do not like rallies. And based on what I see from this vantage point, I do not like most of you. What I do like is breakfast food. JJ's has very good breakfast food, so it should remain open.
jokes.setup: Ron is giving a rally speech ostensibly in support of JJ's Diner
jokes.punchline: He immediately insults the crowd, then delivers the entire logical case for JJ's in two sentences with no appeal to emotion or community
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the better Ron Swanson moments in the series. The structure is perfect: he violates every convention of rally speeches in the opening line, then delivers a logical argument so stripped of sentiment that it's anti-inspirational and somehow more inspiring for it. 'Based on what I see from this vantage point, I do not like most of you' is extraordinary — it's the crowd he's supposedly rallying! The pivot to 'What I do like is breakfast food' is a masterclass in comedic misdirection. This absolutely earns an 8+ craft score: character integration is 9.5 because no other character could give this speech, economy is near-perfect, structure is inverted in the best way.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I've been asked to come here today to inspire you, but I have to be honest with you. You all disgust me. You're weak, you're soft, and you're everything that's wrong with this country.

jokes.text: Please do not approach me on the street after this event and attempt to talk to me. Our similarities begin and end with this single issue.
jokes.setup: Ron is wrapping up his rally speech
jokes.punchline: Instead of a rallying close, he pre-emptively rejects any ongoing relationship with the audience
jokes.explanation: A perfect capper to Ron's rally speech. 'Our similarities begin and end with this single issue' is a line that could be a T-shirt. It's deeply Ron: he came, he made his case, and now he's erecting walls. The anti-community speech at a community rally is the joke. Earns 8.5 craft — slightly behind Joke 34 only because that one had the bigger structural subversion; this is the finishing blow that lands slightly softer but is arguably more quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And if you see me out in public, do not approach me. I will not acknowledge you. In fact, I'm going to take steps to avoid you. I'm installing a small periscope in my car so I can see over obstacles without being seen myself.

jokes.text: Exactly. (responding to being told 'Jonathan Karate' isn't in the appointment book)
jokes.setup: Andy has made an appointment under 'Jonathan Karate' — presumably to seem more intimidating or serious
jokes.punchline: 'Exactly' — as if the absence from the appointment book is itself a feature, implying Jonathan Karate is so serious he operates off the books
jokes.explanation: One-word punchline that does a lot. 'Exactly' implies an entire mythology Andy has built around Jonathan Karate — ghost-like, unscheduled, unannounced. It's the confidence of a man who fully inhabits his own fiction. Economy score is near-perfect: one word delivers the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.line: I don't have a Jonathan Karate in the appointment book.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Perfect. My secret identity is working.

jokes.text: Jonathan Karate confessional: 'Occasionally on my show, we deal with real issues like bullying, peer pressure, or holding in farts.'
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining the serious alter-ego he uses for Very Special Episodes of his kids' show
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of serious issues culminates in 'holding in farts' — a real health topic but an absurd climax to bullying and peer pressure
jokes.explanation: The rule of three with an absurdist pivot: bullying, peer pressure, and then... holding in farts. The first two are classically Very Special Episode topics; the third is what Andy thinks belongs in the same category. It's character-specific because only Andy's show would treat fart retention as a serious social issue.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Including this decidedly unserious bodily function

jokes.text: Oh, baby. That feels amazing. But I'm sorry, I'm gonna have to go. I have to meet Rick and TC at the King Kamehameha Club. Higgins is missing.
jokes.setup: Andy (as Jonathan Karate) arrives to confront Dennis Feinstein; Dennis is mid-conversation on the phone
jokes.punchline: Dennis's phone call is a dense web of obscure references (King Kamehameha Club, Higgins missing) that parody Magnum P.I. while establishing his bizarre social world
jokes.explanation: The Magnum P.I. reference (Higgins, King Kamehameha Club, TC) is a niche but well-deployed bit that adds to Dennis Feinstein's absurd villainy. Works better for older viewers who recognize the references. The casual 'Higgins is missing' as a reason to bail is the comedic peak of the exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I need to make this meeting quick. I have to go end my father's life support.

jokes.text: Well, make it quick. I gotta go pull the plug on my dad in 10 minutes.
jokes.setup: Andy/Jonathan Karate has demanded Dennis's attention
jokes.punchline: Dennis casually mentions he has to pull the plug on his father as a competing time commitment — stated with zero emotional weight
jokes.explanation: Perfectly dark. 'Gotta go pull the plug on my dad in 10 minutes' is delivered as if it were a lunch appointment — the casualness is what makes it horrifying and funny. This is prime Dennis Feinstein: he's not evil because he's sad or complex, he's evil because he just doesn't register normal human stakes. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Real estate prices in this turd town are through the roof. I'm gonna turn that place into an elbow art salon and make a killing.
jokes.setup: Dennis explains why he bought JJ's Diner
jokes.punchline: 'Elbow art salon' — a completely made-up and absurd boutique concept that is exactly what a Dennis Feinstein business would be
jokes.explanation: 'Elbow art salon' is the absurdist invention that makes this joke work — it's specific enough to feel real and ridiculous enough to be funny. Dennis is the kind of person who would open an elbow art salon because it's expensive, exclusive, and useless.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's probably not a good idea to wear this cologne around children. It'll make their eyes water and burn their skin.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But that's what makes it so good!

jokes.text: Psych! (after telling the crowd JJ's can stay, then revealing he lied)
jokes.setup: Dennis appears to relent at the rally; crowd cheers
jokes.punchline: He says 'Psych!' — an aggressively childish betrayal of the crowd's hope, followed by a gleeful monologue about greed
jokes.explanation: The use of 'Psych!' — a 1990s slang term — by an adult businessman at a public rally is a perfect character choice. It speaks to Dennis's arrested development and genuine malice. The crowd's hope and immediate betrayal is classic cringe-discomfort territory.

dialogue.speaker: Tour Guide
dialogue.line: And over here on the left, you can see where Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie live together.

jokes.text: Do you think I care about how much you love this stupid diner? I bought it for a song and I'm gonna sell it for a mint and you can all just sit there pulling on your puds.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just pulled off the Psych moment; he now delivers his villain manifesto
jokes.punchline: 'Pulling on your puds' as the insult he lands on — an archaic, weird phrase that feels authentically Dennis
jokes.explanation: The 'pulling on your puds' phrasing is the comedic detail that saves this from being generic villain speech. 'Bought it for a song, sell it for a mint' is a cliché, but it fits Dennis's character to speak in clichés mixed with bizarre idioms.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I want you to bedazzle my elbow. But I'm talking full coverage — I want rhinestones so big and so bright that when I'm at a club, people think my elbow is a disco ball. I want my elbow to be more sparkly than a vampire in sunlight. I'm talking about a level of bling that makes Mr. T look like a minimalist.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. Give me your boos! I am nourished by your hatred!
jokes.setup: The crowd is booing Dennis after his betrayal
jokes.punchline: Dennis actively solicits boos and declares he is 'nourished by hatred' — turning antagonism into self-care
jokes.explanation: 'I am nourished by your hatred' is the best Dennis Feinstein line in the episode and earns its 8+ score. The phrase perfectly crystallizes his character: he's not just indifferent to hatred, he metabolizes it. The 'Give me your boos!' as an active demand transforms the crowd from threat to resource. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific — this line could only come from Dennis Feinstein. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in precision and quotability, slightly above it in character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Salon Worker
dialogue.line: We offer eye surgery combined with a manicure. It's called a 'Nail-LASIK.' We remove cataracts while filing your cuticles.

jokes.text: Release the Hounds! / What hounds? / The Hounds is an FDA-rejected cologne I've been working on that makes everything smell like wet dog. Make it rain!
jokes.setup: Dennis dramatically calls for 'The Hounds' as a weapon against the crowd
jokes.punchline: The Hounds is an unapproved cologne that smells like wet dog — the subversion of the threat (actual dogs → chemical smell attack) is absurd, and 'FDA-rejected' suggests they tested it and it failed
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's top three jokes. The misdirection is masterful: 'Release the Hounds' is a Simpsons-coded villain cliché — you expect dogs — and instead you get an FDA-rejected cologne that smells like wet dog. The FDA-rejected detail does so much work: it implies the product was tested, submitted, and specifically rejected because it smells like wet dog. 'Make it rain!' as a command to spray cologne on a crowd is the perfect absurdist escalation. Earns its 8.5 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Of course you can stay. I'd be happy to help out an old friend.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Just kidding. No you can't. Get out.

jokes.text: Ooh! I gotta go kill my dad. Let's go.
jokes.setup: Dennis has deployed his cologne; he now wraps up his villainous rally appearance
jokes.punchline: He now says 'kill my dad' rather than the earlier 'pull the plug' — escalating the callousness with a more violent verb
jokes.explanation: Great callback that escalates the earlier dark joke: 'pull the plug' becomes 'kill my dad' with cheerful casualness. The verbal upgrade mirrors the escalating chaos of the scene. Economy is near-perfect — it's five words that close the scene and call back to an earlier beat.

jokes.text: What if we steal the keys to Feinstein's building, break in, and TP his office, film the whole thing. We'd definitely get on a prank show.
jokes.setup: Leslie is apologizing for the failed rally; people are looking for alternatives
jokes.punchline: Andy's elaborate plan has nothing to do with saving the diner — it's designed to get them on a prank show
jokes.explanation: Andy's plan being a means to get on a prank show rather than help JJ is very Andy. The confidence of 'we'd definitely get on a prank show' is the best detail. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You want a villain? I'll give you a villain!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I am the villain of this story, and I embrace it fully!

jokes.text: Ooh. Water makes it worse.
jokes.setup: Someone tries to wash off the Hounds cologne with water.
jokes.punchline: Water makes the wet-dog smell worse — a logical extension of the cologne joke that pays off practically.
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the Hounds cologne joke. The logic is perfect — wet dog smell getting worse with water — and the discovery is communicated twice ('water makes it worse' echoed) for comedic effect. Functional and well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Release the Hounds!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's actually a terrible cologne, not actual dogs.

jokes.text: This is the hottest restaurant in LA. All the sushi is made from fish previously owned by celebrities.
jokes.setup: Tom and Donna are at an exclusive LA restaurant
jokes.punchline: The gimmick is fish 'previously owned by celebrities' — as if celebrity provenance is a culinary value-add
jokes.explanation: The concept of celebrity-owned sushi is a sharp satire of LA luxury culture and the absurdity of provenance-based prestige. 'Previously owned by celebrities' applies the logic of celebrity memorabilia to food, which is genuinely novel and specific to the LA setting.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go now.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But remember what I said about the life support machine.

jokes.text: This is Charlize Theron's yellowtail, here we have Paul Reiser's salmon, and Peter Bogdanovich's saltwater eel. Enjoy.
jokes.setup: The celebrity-fish concept is being delivered
jokes.punchline: The escalating obscurity of the celebrities: Charlize Theron (A-list) → Paul Reiser (B-list 90s sitcom actor) → Peter Bogdanovich (classic Hollywood director, very niche) — the decreasing fame matches the increasingly obscure fish
jokes.explanation: The joke gets funnier as the celebrities get more obscure. Going from Charlize Theron to Peter Bogdanovich is a deliberate structural choice — the restaurant supposedly serves the hottest celebrities' fish but by the third item you're at a 1970s French New Wave-adjacent director. Rewatch bonus because comedy nerds will appreciate the Bogdanovich specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, why does it smell worse?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh no. Water intensifies it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Of course it does.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We're trapped.

jokes.text: Mmm! Bogdano-delish.
jokes.setup: Tasting Peter Bogdanovich's fish
jokes.punchline: 'Bogdano-delish' — a portmanteau of Bogdanovich and delicious, delivered with sincere satisfaction
jokes.explanation: 'Bogdano-delish' is a quick, fun wordplay moment. Earns points for economy and the specificity of the Bogdanovich reference. Tom Haverford's fondness for combining words makes this feel character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is Bogdanovich!

jokes.text: Oh, damn. I was secretly hoping you got me the shoes Jaden Smith wears in Hitch 2: Son of a Hitch.
jokes.setup: Donna says she has advice rather than a gift
jokes.punchline: Tom's specific fantasy gift — shoes from a fictional sequel to Hitch, worn by Jaden Smith — is the kind of hyper-specific cultural confection only Tom could dream up
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford. The joke works on multiple levels: the existence of 'Hitch 2: Son of a Hitch' as a fictional sequel, Jaden Smith as Tom's celebrity obsession, and wanting specifically the shoes he wears in it. The level of detail suggests Tom has thought about this at length. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Donna, this is incredible. Did you get this from that guy who makes up movie sequels? Because I'm pretty sure I saw 'Die Hard 5: Die Hardest' advertised at the mall.

jokes.text: Thanks, Donna, it's a great gift. / Almost forgot. I did get you them shoes from Hitch 2!
jokes.setup: Tom thanks Donna for the advice-as-gift; Donna said she didn't buy anything
jokes.punchline: Donna DID buy the Hitch 2 shoes — the impossible gift exists, doubling down on the absurdity of the earlier fantasy
jokes.explanation: Great callback structure: the setup established an impossible/absurd wish, and the payoff delivers it — in a show where Treat Yo' Self exists, of course Donna got the Hitch 2 shoes. 'Oh, snap!' as Tom's reaction is perfectly on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Listen, you want relationship advice? It's simple. Treat yo' self.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: But that's for material things. For emotional stuff, you gotta treat the other person. Treat them with respect, honesty, and communication.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? Treat yo' self anyway. You'll need it after all those conversations.

jokes.text: Look behind you, but don't be obvious. / Can I get the 'me' soft shell crab? / Josh Groban! He's eating his own sushi! That's the most baller thing I've ever seen!
jokes.setup: Donna points out a celebrity eating at the restaurant; they spot Josh Groban
jokes.punchline: Josh Groban ordering the 'me' sushi — the celebrity sushi named after himself — and Tom calling it 'the most baller thing I've ever seen'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the celebrity sushi bit is exceptional. The joke works on a structural level (the bit pays off), a character level (Josh Groban as the unexpected celebrity), and a conceptual level (a celebrity eating their own sushi named after them). 'The most baller thing I've ever seen' from Tom — a man who has been to Beverly Hills today — is the perfect reaction. Earns its 8.5 craft score: the setup across multiple jokes, the specific celebrity choice, the 'me' soft shell crab phrasing. One of the episode's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that Josh Groban? Josh Groban is eating the branzino!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I caught that fish. That beautiful fish came from my restaurant, and now Josh Groban is eating it. This is the best day of my life.

jokes.text: Welcome to Beachview Terrace, the sad, unsalvageable, broken-down armpit of Pawnee.
jokes.setup: Leslie is introducing a run-down neighborhood as a potential solution
jokes.punchline: Her description is exhaustively negative — 'sad, unsalvageable, broken-down armpit' — with zero spin, the opposite of her usual boosterism
jokes.explanation: Funny primarily because it's Leslie saying it — Leslie Knope calling something 'unsalvageable' is against her nature. The triple-adjective pile-up ('sad, unsalvageable, broken-down armpit') has good comic rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? Beachview Terrace should really be called Mold Spore Inhalation Pavilion, because that's what you get when you live there.

jokes.text: We sent a street cleaner through here a few months ago, raccoons ate the wheels right off it.
jokes.setup: They're describing failed attempts to improve Beachview Terrace
jokes.punchline: Raccoons ate the wheels off the street cleaner — implying wildlife so aggressive and resourceful it defeats municipal equipment
jokes.explanation: A good specific gag that builds the neighborhood's mythology. The image of raccoons eating wheels is vivid and funny. Good economy — one sentence delivers a complete comic picture.

dialogue.speaker: Real Estate Agent
dialogue.line: And here we have the master bedroom with its original 1970s wood paneling and a charming water stain that really adds character to the ceiling. The windows are sealed shut to preserve the authentic drafty feel, and that mysterious smell? That's just the bones of the house settling. In the kitchen, you'll notice the appliances are all avocado green—very retro, very in right now. The refrigerator hasn't worked since 2003, but it's a wonderful conversation starter. And this electrical outlet here sparks occasionally, which means the wiring is really alive and doing its job. The bathroom features a toilet that runs constantly—it's like having a personal water fountain! Plus, the mold in the corner gives the tiles a lovely tie-dye effect. The basement floods every spring, but that just means you have a built-in swimming pool. And finally, the foundation has some significant cracks, but they add structural character. So, shall we talk about putting in an offer?

jokes.text: Councilman Dexhart represents this district, and 10 years ago, when he was elected, he promised to clean it up. Instead, he just gave it a fancy new name, Beachview Terrace.
jokes.setup: History of the neighborhood is being explained
jokes.punchline: The sum total of Dexhart's improvement was renaming it — pure political satire
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire: the politician's entire achievement was a rebrand. Works as Dexhart characterization (established philanderer/bad politician) and as general political commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? I came up through the hole in the floor. Where did you guys think I came from?

jokes.text: A more accurate name for this place? Medical Waste Butt-Sweat Grove.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just explained Dexhart renamed the area to Beachview Terrace
jokes.punchline: Her counter-proposal: Medical Waste Butt-Sweat Grove — a hilariously unflattering name that stacks two disgusting concepts
jokes.explanation: Leslie being willing to say 'Butt-Sweat Grove' is itself the joke — she's usually such a booster. The compound insult name is well-constructed: 'Medical Waste' is institutional and gross, 'Butt-Sweat' is personal and gross, 'Grove' is the sanitized real-estate suffix. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm in charge now. First order of business: we're eliminating all the vegetables from the menu.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Second order of business: deep frying everything that's left.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Third order of business: we're calling it 'Sweetums Lite.'

jokes.text: We've had this listing for seven years and no one's ever asked to see it. I thought this was a prank call.
jokes.setup: A realtor meets the group at Beachview Terrace
jokes.punchline: Seven years of nobody wanting to see the property; the realtor assumed interest was a prank
jokes.explanation: Functional character bit for a one-scene realtor. The prank call assumption is a good detail. Nothing exceptional, but it lands.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I was a boss for 30 seconds. In that time, I fired three people, made two questionable decisions, and one person cried. It was the best 30 seconds of my life.

jokes.text: This place has everything. Vermin, bullet holes, a hornet's nest.
jokes.setup: Realtor is showing the space
jokes.punchline: The realtor lists the property's 'features' — all of which are serious liabilities — as selling points
jokes.explanation: The three-item escalating list of horrors as real-estate features is a classic comic structure. The hornet's nest as the clincher is the right escalating choice. Efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: We're treating the existing graffiti as equivalent to famous artist's work.

jokes.text: Where'd you come from? / The floor hole.
jokes.setup: A character who hasn't been visible suddenly appears to volunteer for the plan
jokes.punchline: 'The floor hole' — stated flatly as a completely normal origin point
jokes.explanation: Two words: 'The floor hole.' Economy score is perfect — it's the maximum possible comedy per word. The deadpan delivery of an insane non-explanation ('the floor hole' as if the building just has a floor hole and that's fine) is a great absurdist beat. Highly quotable, surprising, and perfectly placed as a transitional gag that gets a big laugh. The rewatch bonus applies because viewers will be listening for it the second time knowing it's coming.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: Look, I invested in this forest land because I saw the potential to make hella skrilla. This deal is trill, and I'm about to be rolling in that green.

jokes.text: LASIK for fingernails? I came up with that. You want it? It's 275. / Yeah. Laser my nails off, please.
jokes.setup: Tom and Donna are getting beauty treatments in Beverly Hills
jokes.punchline: LASIK for fingernails is a completely made-up luxury procedure; Tom immediately orders it without hesitation
jokes.explanation: The joke is both the invented procedure and Tom's zero-questions willingness to have his nails lasered off. LASIK for fingernails is a good absurdist concept because LASIK is itself a well-known procedure applied to an absurd body part. 'Laser my nails off, please' is a great line.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We should donate the land to the city. It's the right thing to do. I mean, think about it—we'd be using our brainium!

jokes.text: In fact, forget it. I wasn't even serious. You've been hoaxed! You've been Tommy-ed!
jokes.setup: Tom has just made himself vulnerable by asking Lucy on a real date and admitting his feelings. As Lucy is about to respond, he loses his nerve.
jokes.punchline: 'You've been Tommy-ed!' — Tom inventing a new verb for his own specific brand of emotional self-sabotage. The pride in the self-made term while fleeing from vulnerability is very Tom.
jokes.explanation: 'You've been Tommy-ed!' is a great character moment and a highly quotable line. Only Tom Haverford would name his vulnerability-escape-hatch maneuver after himself. The self-branding of his own emotional cowardice is perfectly on-character. Strong structure: real emotional moment, panic, self-sabotage, self-promotion all in one beat.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: I'd love to help, but I need to consult with my board first.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: They're at Coachella right now on a lot of molly.

jokes.text: It's about time. We're losing the cranberry salad, effective immediately!
jokes.setup: Tom signs over management of Tom's Bistro to Craig so he can ask Lucy out
jokes.punchline: Craig immediately abuses his new authority to eliminate the cranberry salad — his first act of power is a petty menu change
jokes.explanation: Craig getting power and immediately weaponizing it against the cranberry salad is perfect. The specificity of the cranberry salad (suggesting this is a long-running grievance) and 'effective immediately!' as a power declaration are great. Pure Craig character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: I can upload directly to my smart glasses.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: Which is great because I was watching pornography during the meeting.

jokes.text: Well, I wish my reign had lasted longer, but I'm happy with the decisions I made and the people I fired.
jokes.setup: Tom has reversed the management transfer after Lucy agrees to be his date
jokes.punchline: Craig refers to his minutes-long tenure as a 'reign,' claims to have fired people, and expresses satisfaction — implying he made full use of his brief authority
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Craig Middlebrooks moment. 'I wish my reign had lasted longer' — 'REIGN' for a two-minute management stint — is the perfect Craig word choice. 'The people I fired' implies he actually fired staff in the time available, which is both alarming and completely consistent with Craig's character. Extremely quotable. Earns its 8.2 score: deep character specificity, great economy, surprising structure (the reveal that he actually fired people).

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: He came to us like a loon in a three-piece suit. We didn't ask for him. We didn't want him. But he was ours.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: And when he left, he took a piece of us with him. Specifically, my good stapler and about forty dollars from petty cash.

jokes.text: Plus, the best part, all the buildings come pre-graffitied.
jokes.setup: Leslie/Ben are pitching Beachview Terrace to Gryzzl as a better campus option
jokes.punchline: 'Pre-graffitied' is spun as an asset — turning a blight into a feature for a tech company that would pay for street art
jokes.explanation: 'Pre-graffitied' is a genius compound adjective that skewers tech company aesthetic pretension. The logic is: tech companies pay Banksy for street art credibility — this is that, but free. Strong economy and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, where are my ninjas? I had like... I'm pretty sure I had ninjas.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How is that possible? We have a whole system in place to keep track of them.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I see the problem. The system doesn't work.

jokes.text: That's true. We wouldn't have to hire Banksy.
jokes.setup: Leslie has described the buildings as pre-graffitied
jokes.punchline: Roscoe genuinely considering not having to hire Banksy as a cost-saving measure, confirming their intent to do exactly that
jokes.explanation: Perfect tech company satire: the joke is that Gryzzl WOULD hire Banksy, and this is genuinely a cost consideration for them. Roscoe's earnest agreement makes it land harder. Great callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you knew? You knew the whole time and you didn't tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I wanted to see how long you could go without telling everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron! That's not funny! I've been stressed out of my mind!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It was a little funny.

jokes.text: Okay, but we spent hella skrilla on this trill forest.
jokes.setup: Gryzzl is weighing whether to move their campus to Beachview Terrace
jokes.punchline: 'Hella skrilla' and 'trill forest' — tech-bro slang applied to a serious financial decision about a nature preserve
jokes.explanation: Roscoe's dialect is a reliable source of character comedy. 'Trill forest' is a particularly good coinage for a nature preserve. The slang applied to serious business is the core Gryzzl satirical engine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm going to hug you now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, no. I don't want—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Too late!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Get off me. I'm serious. This is inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You love this and you know it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I absolutely do not.

jokes.text: Here's a far-out idea that just came to the top of my brainium.
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to pitch the idea of donating the forest land to the National Park Service
jokes.punchline: 'Brainium' — Leslie has adopted Gryzzl/Roscoe's linguistic style to speak their language, using a made-up word
jokes.explanation: Leslie code-switching into Roscoe's dialect with 'brainium' is a smart character beat — she's pragmatically adjusting her communication style. 'Brainium' is also a legitimately funny fake word.

jokes.text: That would be pretty dope. And you could get some baller tax breaks that could help you with that mad stank construction cost.
jokes.setup: Leslie continues pitching in Gryzzl-speak.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's continued deployment of tech-bro slang — 'baller tax breaks,' 'mad stank construction cost' — reaches its peak with 'mad stank,' which she uses to mean 'very large/smelly,' conflating the slang term with its literal meaning.
jokes.explanation: 'Mad stank construction cost' is Leslie's slang at peak awkward authenticity. The continued adoption of Gryzzl dialect pays off the running bit. 'Stank' in a financial context is a nice absurd collision.

jokes.text: I don't know. / I'm sorry, I can't. I can't say these words...
jokes.setup: Someone is trying to continue speaking in tech-bro slang while pitching to Gryzzl
jokes.punchline: They physically cannot continue — the language is too much for them to maintain
jokes.explanation: A reaction beat that works on the physical level — whoever is speaking cannot keep up the slang performance. Gets a chuckle for the authentic discomfort with the dialect.

jokes.text: And truthfully, they're all shrooming super hard at Coachella right now.
jokes.setup: Roscoe explains he needs to consult his board, legal counsel, and senior advisory team
jokes.punchline: They're all on mushrooms at Coachella — stated as a straightforward logistical obstacle, not an embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Excellent tech satire. The board of directors being unavailable because they're 'shrooming super hard at Coachella' is funny because it's said with zero shame or self-awareness — it's just a scheduling conflict. The specificity of 'shrooming SUPER hard' (not just shrooming — SUPER hard) is the detail that pushes it into great territory. Earns its 8.0 craft score.

jokes.text: Andy has a meeting? / Upload it to my GryzzlGlass. Left eye. I'm watching porn with my right eye.
jokes.setup: Andy mentions having a meeting; Roscoe casually offers to stream something to his smart glasses
jokes.punchline: Left eye is for uploads; right eye is currently occupied with pornography — stated as a normal operational detail
jokes.explanation: The logic of the GryzzlGlass having a dedicated porn eye while the left eye handles meetings is a genuinely novel tech-satire concept. The matter-of-fact delivery makes it funnier — he's not embarrassed, it's just multitasking. Earns its 8.0: the specificity of left vs. right eye is the detail that elevates it from shock comedy to clever absurdism.

jokes.text: Upload it to my GryzzlGlass. Left eye. I'm watching porn with my right eye.
jokes.setup: Roscoe is leaving and asks for something to be uploaded to his GryzzlGlass (Google Glass parody).
jokes.punchline: The specification of 'left eye' followed immediately by 'I'm watching porn with my right eye' — the casual multitasking of business and pornography via smart glasses — is a great Gryzzl tech-dystopia beat.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logical extension of smart glasses technology — two eyes, two screens, one for work, one for porn — is delivered with complete business-casual normalcy. 'Left eye' as the professional designation implies a whole private-public dichotomy infrastructure. Excellent economy, originality, and character integration.

jokes.text: Who did this? / We did. One way or another, Jonathan Karate always gets his man.
jokes.setup: Something has been done to Dennis's building/office (implied by context)
jokes.punchline: Andy (as Jonathan Karate) claims credit with maximum gravitas: 'one way or another, Jonathan Karate always gets his man'
jokes.explanation: Andy fully inhabiting Jonathan Karate's gravitas for a children's TV character is charming. 'Always gets his man' is a great crime drama cliché applied to whatever minor mischief just occurred.

jokes.text: Wait, where's... Hey, guys, where's Gavin? Gav? Wait, stop. There were supposed to be six ninjas. Where's Gavin? Gavin? / Who was Gavin's buddy? Caleb, come on, dude. / Why do we even have a buddy system? Is he in the bathroom? You need to tell me if Gavin is pooping. / No, do not laugh, okay? You're not even Caleb. You're Gavin. You're Caleb. If you're Caleb, where's Hunter? Hunter! Hunter! / Okay, who was Hunter's buddy? Hmm? Oh, I was. Oh, crap.
jokes.setup: Andy/Jonathan Karate's dramatic exit is immediately undercut by the discovery that a ninja child is missing
jokes.punchline: The escalating chaos of missing children (Gavin → Hunter) undoes all of Jonathan Karate's cool, culminating in Andy realizing HE was Hunter's buddy and abandoned him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest extended sequences. The joke structure is a perfect deflation of Andy's earlier cool: he just walked out narrating himself like a crime drama, and now he can't locate kindergartners. The escalation from Gavin → Hunter → Andy realizing he was Hunter's buddy is beautifully constructed. 'You need to tell me if Gavin is pooping' is the standout line — it's specific, real, and reveals that Andy takes the buddy system seriously despite failing it completely. 'Oh, I was. Oh, crap.' as the realization lands perfectly. Earns its 8.3 craft score: near-perfect structure and character integration.

jokes.text: There were supposed to be six ninjas. Where's Gavin? Gavin? / Who was Gavin's buddy? / Caleb, come on, dude.
jokes.setup: Andy/Jonathan Karate is trying to make a dramatic exit with his ninja children.
jokes.punchline: The dramatic exit falls apart as Andy discovers a ninja is missing, revealing the 'buddy system' and escalating chaos of trying to wrangle the children.
jokes.explanation: The Jonathan Karate escape sequence falling apart due to a missing child is a great comedic deflation of Andy's self-serious action-hero persona. The buddy system reveal and escalating head count are well-paced.

jokes.text: You're not even Caleb. You're Gavin. You're Caleb. If you're Caleb, where's Hunter? Hunter! Hunter!
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to account for all his ninjas after Gavin went missing.
jokes.punchline: The escalating confusion — misidentifying children, the buddy system breaking down completely, the discovery of yet another missing child (Hunter) — is a well-escalated chaotic comedy sequence.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — we went from one missing ninja to two, and Andy's methodical buddy-system approach is completely unraveling. The rising panic in 'Hunter! Hunter!' is very Andy: total commitment to a system that he himself is failing to maintain.

jokes.text: A wise woman once told me that whenever you and I team up, good things happen. Also, they called three hours ago, said they approved the plan, and asked me to begin drawings for the renovation.
jokes.setup: Ron is comforting a worried Leslie with a philosophical statement about their partnership
jokes.punchline: He buried the actual good news — that Gryzzl already approved everything three hours ago — after the inspirational speech
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect Ron Swanson joke. He watched Leslie worry for three hours — having already received good news — because he's Ron Swanson, and that's exactly what Ron would do. The reveal structure is ideal: the warm setup about partnership seems like the punchline, then the real punchline arrives deadpan. 'Also,' as the pivot is perfect — one word before delivering a bombshell. Earns its 8.0: deeply character-specific, well-structured, warm-funny rather than just funny.

jokes.text: I don't know, Ron. I mean, it's been a week. It might not work... But what if it doesn't?
jokes.setup: Leslie is spiraling with anxiety about whether Gryzzl will approve the plan.
jokes.punchline: Ron lets her spiral for a moment — the comedy is in Leslie's inability to sit with uncertainty, which is deeply character-specific.
jokes.explanation: More of a character/dramatic beat than a strong joke. Leslie's anxiety is authentic and well-played, but the humor is mild. Functional scene work.

jokes.text: You jerk. You sat on that news and let me stew here for three hours? / Yup. / You jerk! We did it! / You jerk. / Yep. Congratulations.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just learned Ron withheld good news for three hours
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'You jerk' punctuates her emotional whiplash — joy and betrayal mixed together — while Ron's 'Yup' and 'Yep. Congratulations.' are perfectly minimal
jokes.explanation: Beautiful character exchange. The 'You jerk' repeated three times — shifting from anger to joy to affection — is a great comedic structure. Ron's 'Yup' and 'Yep. Congratulations.' are pure Ron: minimal, unapologetic, warm in their own way. This is the emotional payoff of the Leslie-Ron dynamic and it works as both comedy and character moment. Earns its 8.1 craft score.

jokes.text: I do not approve of this. / Don't care.
jokes.setup: Someone is objecting to something happening at the end of the episode (possibly Craig objecting to having his authority revoked)
jokes.punchline: 'Don't care.' — an absolute dismissal
jokes.explanation: A quick capper gag. 'Don't care' is economical and funny as a final beat, but without clear character attribution and context from the transcript, it's hard to score highly. Works as a button.

tmdb_overview: Leslie holds a rally in an attempt to keep JJ's Diner from closing. Tom surprises Donna with the ultimate pre-wedding gift.
insight: Final season nostalgia carries 67 jokes through a restaurant-saving plot at moderate velocity.
